sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Relational foundation models are rapidly expanding what single pretrained model can learn from databases. Recent models transfer across unseen schemas and tasks [Ranjan et al., 2026a, Hudovernik et al., 2026], scale through synthetic relational pretraining [Kothapalli et al., 2026], and adapt to new prediction problems from context [Wang et al., 2026, Ranjan et al., 2026b]. Yet these advances largely share the same learning interface, using relational database state to predict target y. This formulation treats the database primarily as dataset. In many applications, however, the database is also the observable state of running system, shaped by users, software, and operational processes [Klein and Hoffart, 2025, 2026]. Choosing an action requires asking how it would change that state. This calls for an action-conditioned transition model from (St, At) to St+1, the core abstraction of world modeling that allows model to imagine how system evolves under candidate actions [Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018, Ding et al., 2025, Hafner et al., 2025]. We ask whether relational learning can make this shift from prediction to world modeling. 1 Consider an order that is predicted to arrive late. Knowing that it will be late does not tell us what will change if we expedite it. In Figure 1a, expediting O-4711 updates its order and shipment, consumes the remaining inventory, and pushes back O-4712 although the action does not name it. Similar what-if questions arise in prescriptive process monitoring and business-process simulation [Dasht Bozorgi et al., 2023, Camargo et al., 2020, 2022, Chapela-Campa et al., 2025]. We represent these direct and propagated changes as sparse set of structured edits St (Figure 1b). Each edit specifies an operation, its relational location, and value when needed. Applying the edits updates the affected records without regenerating unchanged data. The action specifies what is done, but the system dynamics determine where its effects propagate and what values result. These dynamics depend on operational rules that may not be apparent from the database records [Klein and Hoffart, 2025, 2026]. We call relational system with particular schema, set of actions, and transition mechanism world. Its executions are observable, but we assume its mechanism is hidden. In controlled experiment across 200 pairs of worlds, executing the same action from identical relational states produces different structured edits in 65% of probes. The current state and action therefore leave the consequence ambiguous across worlds. Past executions provide evidence about how actions behave in the current world. Intuitively, states show what system looks like, while transitions show how it behaves. Learning from these executions is often approached by discovering or calibrating simulator for particular process [Camargo et al., 2020, 2022, Chapela-Campa et al., 2025]. In-context system identification offers another route. model trained across class of dynamical systems can infer the behavior of new one from its observed history [Forgione et al., 2023, Rufolo et al., 2025]. We ask whether the same idea can be extended to relational systems. Instead of fitting separate model for every new world, single pretrained model would use observed executions as context to predict the outcome of new action in that world (Figure 1c). We realize this idea with TabWM (Tabular World Model), trained across executable relational worlds generated by WorldRel. WorldRel extends the PluRel relational prior [Kothapalli et al., 2026] with executable actions and world-specific transition mechanisms. Within task, the observed executions and query share the same dynamics, while those dynamics vary across tasks. This extends prior-data fitted learning [Müller et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2026] from static relational prediction to action-conditioned transitions. TabWM preserves relational structure together with which actions produced which observed consequences. It then predicts the consequence of new action as sparse set of edits that specify what changes, where it changes, and what value is written. At test time, the model adapts to new world through observed executions without updating its parameters. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no behavioral context to 0.685 with 64 observed executions, where correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Context remains useful when action mappings, schemas, and mechanism compositions change, and the same pattern persists when relational structure and values are derived from real databases. single pretrained model can therefore improve its predictions from experience in new world without updating its parameters. world model is useful not only for predicting what happens next, but for deciding what to do next. Because TabWM predicts explicit edits, it can roll candidate actions forward into future relational states and compare the resulting trajectories through model-based planning [Hafner et al., 2019, Chua et al., 2018]. At fixed three-step horizon, expanding the candidate pool from 16 to 64 improves the selected return in 30 of 40 held-out worlds. This gives TabWM two ways to improve at test time. More observed executions improve consequence prediction, while broader search over predicted futures improves action selection.

sections.title: 2.1 Relational Worlds
sections.content: We study relational system whose execution rules are hidden from the learner. Its structure and dynamics define world = (Σw, Aw, ρw, Tw), (1) where Σw specifies the tables, columns, and relational links, Aw the available actions, ρw the distribution of initial execution states, and Tw the transition mechanism. These components remain fixed while the database 2 state changes through execution. An action At specifies its type and arguments, which can reference records or supply values [Pasula et al., 2007, Martínez et al., 2016]. The database is the learners observation of the system, not its complete execution state. We write St = Obs(Xt), where Xt also contains any unobserved information used during execution. Starting from X0 ρw, executing an action produces St Tw( Xt, At). (2) The consequence St is variable-size set of edits that update numeric or categorical attributes, insert records, or delete them. Each edit specifies an operation, its relational target, and any required values or record contents. Numeric updates specify resulting values, not increments. The target records the changes caused during action execution, excluding separately generated external changes. It is empty when execution produces no edits.

sections.title: 2.2 Predicting from Behavioral Context
sections.content: The learner receives behavioral context CK = {(Si, Ai, Si)}K i=1 of observed transitions and query (Sq, Aq) from the same world. The demonstrations include observed consequences, while the query consequence Sq is withheld. The learner predicts (cid:100)Sq = fθ(CK , Sq, Aq). (3) Demonstrations and queries share dynamics but come from separate episodes, each starting from fresh initial state X0 ρw. Context therefore provides evidence across executions, not the querys own history. The parameters θ are learned across worlds and held fixed for an unseen test world [Forgione et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2026]. Adaptation occurs through the observed transitions, without access to executable rules or complete execution states. We first test why this evidence is needed by holding the query state and action fixed while changing the execution rules.

sections.title: 3 Same State, Different Consequences
sections.content: Similar database states can arise under different operational rules [Klein and Hoffart, 2026]. We test whether this ambiguity remains when the observed state and action are both identical. We pair worlds that share schema, initial-state distribution, observable action definitions, and set of transition mechanisms. We change only which mechanism each action invokes. We sample 200 pairs without filtering and draw 64 matched initial states per pair, checking that all database tables agree elementwise. Each probe executes the same valid action, including its arguments, in both worlds with the same random seed, giving (S0, A) w0 S(0) and (S0, A) w1 S(1). We compare the complete edit sets, including each edits operation, relational target, and required values or record contents. The observed states match in all 12,800 paired probes, yet the edit sets differ in 65.0% of them. Figure 2 shows how this disagreement rate varies across world pairs. Figure 2 Edit-set disagreement under identical states and actions. The dashed line marks the mean across world pairs (65.0%), with shading indicating bootstrap uncertainty in the mean. Observed transitions link actions to the changes they produced in the current world. They provide evidence about the execution rules that the state alone does not reveal. We next build model that learns across worlds to use this evidence when predicting new execution.

sections.title: 4 TabWM: A Tabular World Model for Relational Systems
sections.content: The ambiguity in 3 turns consequence prediction into an identification problem: the same observed state and action can behave differently across worlds, so model must use previous executions to infer which dynamics are active before predicting new one. TabWM learns this inference across relational worlds while predicting the consequence itself rather than the hidden transition mechanism. Its training distribution varies dynamics across worlds, its encoder preserves the behavioral evidence within each observed execution, and its decoder converts that evidence into sparse set of structured edits. Because these edits define the resulting relational state, the same model can also be applied recursively to imagine subsequent actions.

sections.title: 4.1 Learning Across Relational Worlds
sections.content: Learning to identify new worlds dynamics from context requires training tasks in which behavior remains consistent within world and varies across worlds. We construct such tasks with WorldRel, which extends the relational prior of PluRel [Kothapalli et al., 2026] with executable actions and world-specific transition mechanisms. Each sampled world fixes relational schema, an action interface, an initial-state distribution, and transition mechanism. Observed executions and the query are drawn from separate episodes of the same world, while worlds are resampled across tasks. describes this executable-world prior in detail. The query consequence provides the prediction target, while the observed executions reveal which behavior applies in the current world. Following prior-data fitted learning [Müller et al., 2022], training across these tasks teaches single model to use behavioral context instead of relying on one fixed actionconsequence mapping. This amortizes action-conditioned system identification across worlds [Forgione et al., 2023]. At test time, TabWM adapts to an unseen world through its observed executions without updating its parameters.

sections.title: 4.2 Encoding Relational Transitions
sections.content: Using executions as evidence requires preserving more than the database state alone. The representation must retain how records are linked, which action and consequence belong to the same execution, and how an observed value changed before and after that action. We initialize TabWMs relational encoder from the pretrained Relational Transformer [Ranjan et al., 2026a], using weights learned from PluRel-generated relational databases [Kothapalli et al., 2026]. This provides an initial representation of relational structure, which TabWM adapts together with its transition-specific components to action-conditioned prediction. For each execution, we collect an action-centered neighborhood by following primaryand foreign-key links from the records referenced by the action, subject to cell budget. Cells retain their column identity, type, and value, while textual identifiers use deterministic hash embeddings rather than pretrained language encoder. The action is represented as pseudo-row linked to the records bound by its arguments, with scalar and categorical arguments represented as action cells. We encode the correspondence within each execution. Demonstrated edits are attached to the records they modify. Role embeddings distinguish state, action, and consequence cells, while transition-index embeddings mark which elements belong to the same execution. For observed updates, shared table, record, and column identities align the before-state cell with its demonstrated edit. Together, these connections preserve relational structure, execution membership, and the before-and-after evidence needed to interpret the query. Packing the behavioral context and query gives Uq = Pack(CK , Sq, Aq), Hq = Encθ(Uq), (4) where the query consequence is withheld and Hq contains the resulting contextual representations.

sections.title: 5 Inferring Dynamics in Unseen Worlds
sections.content: If observed executions reveal how actions behave in world, prediction should improve as more executions from that world enter context, without changing the model parameters. We test this by varying the amount of behavioral context available to TabWM. Evaluation. Each task provides observed stateactionconsequence transitions and separate query from held-out WorldRel world. The context sweep uses 250 worlds and three queries per world at each {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. Support F1 measures whether the predicted edits have the correct operations and relational locations, while Edit F1 additionally requires their written values to be correct. Value MAE measures numeric error once the correct location has been identified. The numeric tolerance and remaining scoring details are given in B. Observed executions improve both effect localization and complete-edit prediction, while numeric error on correctly located edits falls (Figure 3). Edit F1 reaches 0.705 with 64 executions, up from 0.029 without 5 behavioral context. Edit F1 still improves between 32 and 64 observations, so the context gain has not saturated by 32 executions. We next ask whether other model classes can exploit the same evidence. Flat-GBM and Flat-TabPFN reduce each task to fixed-width candidate-cell features and summaries of observed changes, then predict edits using gradient boosting [Friedman, 2001] or TabPFN [Hollmann et al., 2025]. Qwen3 [Yang et al., 2025a] instead receives textual serialization of the observed executions and query, testing whether general-purpose LLM can infer the current dynamics from the same evidence. Readable identifiers provide Qwen3 with an additional source of information because table, column, categorical, and action names may carry familiar linguistic cues. We therefore evaluate matched readable and opaque renderings of the same tasks. In the opaque view, these identifiers are replaced consistently with arbitrary labels while preserving relational structure, row identities, values, types, and action arguments. The readable view restores the original identifiers. TabWM uses deterministic hash embeddings, so readable strings do not provide pretrained linguistic semantics. All methods are evaluated on the same 60 held-out worlds with one query per world at each {0, 4, 16, 64}, and Qwen3 and TabWM receive the same action-centred cell budget. Under opaque naming, TabWM leads at every context size and reaches 0.687 Edit F1 with 64 observed executions, compared with 0.407 for Qwen3-32B  (Table 1)  . The advantage is already visible in effect localization, where Support F1 is 0.887 for TabWM and 0.753 for Qwen3-32B under the same condition. Restoring readable names benefits Qwen3 substantially more than TabWM, but the complete-edit gap remains. sections.title: 6 Identifying the Active Dynamics
sections.content: Improvement from demonstrations alone does not establish that model has inferred how actions behave in the current world. In-context learners can benefit from demonstrations even when their labels are randomized [Min et al., 2022]. If TabWM is using executions as behavioral evidence, however, preserving which action produced which consequence should be essential. We test this using the paired worlds from 3, where an identical observed state and action can produce different consequences under different hidden dynamics. TabWM receives either intact transitions or corrupted 6 versions of the same observed executions. Shuffling the actions preserves the states and consequences but assigns each consequence to different action. Shuffling the consequences preserves the states and actions but attaches the wrong response to each execution. Both interventions retain the observed components while breaking their correspondence. With 64 observed executions, intact transitions yield 0.664 Edit F1, compared with 0.041 after shuffling actions and 0.006 after shuffling consequences (Figure 4). The context gain therefore depends on observing which consequences followed which actions, rather than simply on seeing additional database states or edit sets. Which executions are most informative for query? At fixed = 16, Edit F1 rises from 0.048 when the queried action is absent from context to 0.403 with one execution of that action and 0.700 with four. This gain is not explained by replaying previous consequences. An explicit per-action template-transfer baseline reaches only 0.169 and 0.216 with one and four matching executions. TabWM therefore uses repeated executions of the queried action to infer how its effect transfers to new relational state ( F.3). We next vary which part of the world changes relative to the pretraining setting. held-out state changes the database state while leaving the surrounding world construction unchanged. permuted action map retains the action vocabulary but reassigns which transition mechanism each action invokes. An unseen schema changes the relational structure, while held-out mechanism composition changes which familiar mechanisms occur together in one world. Figure 4 Behavioral context helps only when action-consequence correspondence is preserved. The permuted action map is particularly diagnostic because the action identities remain unchanged while their effects do not. Edit F1 rises from 0.378 with 16 executions to 0.604 with 64, showing that behavioral context can override the mapping suggested by prior experience and recover the remapped action behavior. Additional executions also improve prediction under the other shifts  (Table 2)  . Relational topology and value distributions are derived from real databases while the action and transition mechanism remain fixed. We first replace the relational structure. With 64 observed executions, Edit F1 is 0.657 on the imported topologies and 0.671 on the matched synthetic worlds. Replacing relational connectivity alone therefore causes little loss. sections.title: 8 From Predicted Consequences to Decisions
sections.content: Comparing actions requires more than predicting one consequence at time. useful world model must imagine possible futures and distinguish which are preferable before acting. We therefore use TabWM as rollout model: predicted edits are applied recursively along candidate action sequences, and the resulting trajectories are scored with the known task objective [Hafner et al., 2019, Chua et al., 2018]. We first ask whether these imagined futures preserve the ordering induced by the true system, and then whether that ordering leads to better choices when more alternatives are available.

sections.title: 8.1 Ranking Candidate Futures
sections.content: At each decision state, we sample shared pool of 64 legal three-step action sequences. TabWM rolls each sequence forward and scores the imagined trajectory using the known world-specific objective, which combines changes in state potential with action costs (B.4). We execute the same sequences in the true simulator to obtain their realized returns. The evaluation contains 160 decision states from 40 held-out worlds, with states and candidate pools shared across context sizes. Spearman correlation is computed within each 64-sequence pool and averaged across decision states. Normalized regret measures, within the same pool, the realized-return gap between the selected candidate and the best available candidate, divided by the pools return span. To separate information about state changes from simpler sources of ranking signal, we use three references. The simulator oracle rolls candidates forward with the true transition mechanism rather than TabWM. The shuffled-context control mismatches demonstrated actions with their observed consequences before prediction, preserving the amount of context while breaking its behavioral correspondence. The no-change control keeps the predicted state fixed, leaving action costs as the only source of variation between sequences. With intact behavioral context, TabWMs imagined ranking becomes increasingly consistent with realized returns  (Table 4)  . With 64 observed executions, its Spearman correlation reaches 0.622, compared with 0.338 after shuffling the actionconsequence correspondence and 0.345 when state changes are ignored altogether. The simulator oracle reaches 0.732. The contrast with the two controls shows that the ranking gain comes from information about how candidate actions change the current world, rather than only from their immediate costs. This separation echoes prior observations that predictive fidelity and control utility need not improve in lockstep [Lambert et al., 2020, Grimm et al., 2020, Zhang et al., 2026b].

Executions provide an informative ordering over candidate futures, while broader search gives that ordering more opportunities to improve the decision.

sections.title: 9 Related Work
sections.content: Relational foundation models. Relational learning has recently moved from task-specific models toward reusable models that transfer across databases and prediction tasks. Griffin [Wang et al., 2025], the Relational Transformer [Ranjan et al., 2026a], and KumoRFM-2 [Hudovernik et al., 2026] learn transferable representations directly over relational data, while synthetic pretraining and in-context formulations further support adaptation across databases [Kothapalli et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026, Hayler et al., 2026]. Despite these different approaches, the learning interface remains largely predictive, with relational context used to infer targets or properties of database records. TabWM changes what is inferred from context: observed executions provide evidence about how actions change those records. Learning dynamics from behavioral context. Once the target becomes an action-conditioned transition, our setting connects to work on learning action effects and identifying dynamics from experience. Relational action models learn structured or stochastic effects for planning [Pasula et al., 2007, Martínez et al., 2016], while context-conditioned dynamics models adapt prediction from recent transitions [Lee et al., 2020]. Priordata fitted learning provides broader route to amortizing such inference across tasks [Müller et al., 2022], including models trained across synthetic dynamical systems that infer new behavior from input-output histories [Forgione et al., 2023, Rufolo et al., 2025]. TabWM brings this form of identification to relational systems, where an action can induce sparse changes that propagate across linked records. World models for operational systems. In operational systems, the transition mechanism itself may not be apparent from the values stored in the database [Klein and Hoffart, 2025, 2026]. Enterprise workflow benchmarks expose cascading action effects [Gupta et al., 2026], while process simulators recover executable models from event logs for what-if analysis [Chapela-Campa et al., 2025]. When the active configuration is readable, runtime discovery provides another way to ground predictions in the current system [Nair et al., 2026]. TabWM studies the complementary case in which the mechanism is hidden but its executions are observable, allowing behavior in the current world to be inferred from context.

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: Relational databases can describe not only what system looks like, but also how it changes. TabWM learns from observed executions to predict sparse relational consequences of new actions, adapting through context rather than parameter updates. Because these predictions are explicit edits, they can be composed into candidate futures and used to compare actions before they are taken. More broadly, our results suggest that 9 relational dynamics can be learned in context. Pretraining across executable worlds allows single model to infer action consequences from executions in new world. Limitations & Future Work. Moving from relational prediction to relational world modeling also changes what is required from an evaluation benchmark. Studying behavior from experience requires aligned observations of the relational state before an action, the action itself, and the resulting changes, which current relational benchmarks rarely expose. This motivates our use of executable worlds and suggests natural next step in building datasets around real operational execution traces. Such benchmarks would enable broader evaluation across systems and open the study of how relational models infer, track, and use dynamics from experience.

sections.title: A Extended Discussion
sections.content: Relational foundation models have largely expanded pretraining along the diversity of databases, schemas, and prediction tasks [Ranjan et al., 2026a, Kothapalli et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026]. World modeling introduces another axis: the diversity of behaviors that relate actions to future relational states. Scaling along this axis is not simply matter of observing more database instances. It requires prior that captures reusable patterns of change while allowing their concrete realization to vary across systems. This suggests behavioral diversity as distinct dimension of relational pretraining alongside structural and semantic diversity. broad prior describes which behaviors are plausible, but evidence from the current system is still needed to determine which are active. Observed executions provide one such source by directly connecting actions to realized consequences [Forgione et al., 2023, Rufolo et al., 2025]. Runtime-readable configuration can provide another by exposing rules instantiated in the current system [Nair et al., 2026]. These signals constrain the dynamics in different ways. pretrained prior captures regularities across systems, configuration describes explicitly available rules, and executions reveal their realized behavior under the current state. Combining these sources raises broader question of how relational world model should update its view of the current system when evidence differs in specificity or completeness, and how such evidence should be exposed by operational environments in the first place. Once model can act, the evidence available for identification is no longer fixed. Actions can change both the system and what can be learned about it, connecting planning with ideas from dual control and active identification [Mesbah, 2018]. The relevant uncertainty, however, need not be the uncertainty that contributes most to average transition error. Our planning results show that consequence prediction and action selection improve at different rates, consistent with prior observations that predictive fidelity and control utility need not align perfectly [Lambert et al., 2020, Grimm et al., 2020]. This suggests decision-directed view of identification in which model seeks evidence that can change which futures should be preferred.

sections.title: C Method Details
sections.content: TabWM must preserve two kinds of structure at once: the relational structure of the database and the correspondence between each observed action and its consequence [Ranjan et al., 2026a]. The encoder represents both in shared context, while the decoder predicts the query consequence as set of typed edits and transfers numeric transformations across executions. C.1 Relational Transition Encoding The relational state is represented with the pretrained Relational Transformer backbone [Ranjan et al., 2026a], using weights learned from PluRel-generated relational databases [Kothapalli et al., 2026]. TabWM extends this representation from static relational neighborhood to an execution by placing the state, action, and observed consequence in the same relational context. For each execution, an action-centered neighborhood is collected by following primaryand foreign-key links from the records referenced by the action until the cell budget is reached. Cells retain their column identity, type, and value. Textual identifiers use deterministic hash embeddings rather than pretrained language encoder. This lets the model preserve identity within task without introducing external linguistic semantics. The action is represented as distinguished pseudo-row linked to the records bound by its entity arguments. Scalar and categorical arguments are represented as action cells. Demonstrated edits are attached to the records they modify. Role embeddings distinguish state, action, and consequence cells, while transition identifiers mark which elements belong to the same observed execution. For an updated cell, shared table, row, and column identities align its before-action representation with the edit that follows the action. These connections preserve both relational structure and execution membership. When the demonstrations and query are packed as in Equation 4, the query consequence is withheld while its state and action share attention with the observed executions. The encoder can therefore relate queried action to the current relational state and to before-and-after evidence from the same world. C.2 Structured Edit Prediction An action may change several relational targets or none, and the order of those changes has no meaning. TabWM therefore predicts the consequence as an unordered set using learned edit queries, following DETRstyle set prediction [Carion et al., 2020]. Each query attends to the contextual representation and predicts whether an edit exists, which operation it performs, where it acts, and any value or record contents required by that operation. The predicted operation determines the form of the relational target. Value and state updates point to affected cells, while rowand table-level operations select the corresponding relational objects. Typed output heads predict categorical and numeric contents. The decoder therefore separates identifying what changes from predicting what value results, while keeping both parts within the same edit representation. There is no canonical ordering between predicted slots and reference edits. During training, minimum-cost bipartite matching assigns predicted slots to reference edits using their operation, relational target, and value when applicable. Matched slots receive supervision for the corresponding edit fields, while unmatched slots learn to emit no edit. The supervision is applied to the observed consequence itself. TabWM is not given the hidden transition program that produced it. C.3 Numeric Value Transfer Once numeric target has been identified, the remaining question is how its value should change. The decoder uses visible before-and-after pairs (xr, yr) from previous executions that modify the same relational role. Here xr is the value before the demonstrated action and yr is the value written by its consequence. The edit query, target representation, and query action condition attention over these pairs, allowing the model to select changes that are relevant to the current query rather than treating all observed numeric edits equally. 17 learned path first predicts numeric estimate without assuming particular transformation form. It produces an initial estimate ˆy0 together with residual correction, ˆylearned = ˆy0 + rθ. (12) The contextual representation used for this prediction includes the selected before-and-after evidence and the actions under which those changes were observed. Alongside this learned estimate, TabWM constructs two transformation candidates from the same evidence. Let αr denote normalized attention weights over usable pairs and let and be their weighted means. For query value xq, hadd = xq + αr(yr xr), haff = + β(xq x), (13) (cid:88) where β is bounded weighted least-squares slope. The additive candidate transfers an observed change, while the affine candidate estimates how the outcome varies with the starting value. Both therefore apply transformation inferred from the demonstrations to the query value rather than copying demonstrated outcome. Learned gates combine these candidates with the neural estimate as in Equation 7. This gives the decoder several ways to use the same behavioral evidence. The learned path can represent changes that are not captured by simple arithmetic form, while the additive and affine paths provide direct routes for regularities that transfer cleanly across starting values. Candidate construction uses only visible before-and-after pairs that remain informative after value-domain clipping. The affine candidate additionally requires at least two usable pairs with variation in their starting values. When candidate is unavailable, it contributes no correction to ˆylearned. If no usable numeric evidence is present, prediction falls back to the learned estimate. These choices affect only the value written by numeric edit and do not alter its predicted operation or relational target. The arithmetic paths only modify the value attached to an already selected numeric edit. F.5 isolates their contribution under matched reader training. C.4 Training Details TabWM initializes its relational encoder from the pretrained Relational Transformer used in 4.2. The encoder, structured edit decoder, and numeric value decoder are then optimized jointly on tasks sampled from WorldRel. Each task contains behavioral context and separate query from the same world, with the context size sampled from {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. Training, development, and evaluation use disjoint world seed ranges. For numeric edits, training uses routing curriculum to provide stable target representation while the edit pointers are still inaccurate. After set matching, matched numeric slot may initially read the reference target cell when constructing the value-decoder input. This probability is annealed to zero during training, after which the model uses its own predicted target throughout. sections.title: E The WorldRel Prior
sections.content: A relational world is defined not only by what its database looks like, but by how that database changes under actions. WorldRel turns this distinction into generative prior. Starting from relational databases sampled with PluRel [Kothapalli et al., 2026], it adds executable actions and world-specific transition mechanisms whose effects remain consistent within world and vary across worlds. The resulting tasks expose TabWM to different relational structures and different ways in which those structures can evolve. E.1 Generating Executable Worlds Each sampled world fixes four components: relational schema, an action interface, an initial-state distribution, and transition mechanism. The base relational schema contains between 2 and 12 sampled tables with typed attributes and sampled foreign-key structure. Each world also contains between 4 and 24 actions that bind primary entity and may additionally take entity, scalar, or categorical arguments. Actions can carry state-dependent preconditions and costs. Resetting the world draws fresh relational state while preserving its action interface and dynamics. 19 Table 7 Sources of variation in WorldRel world. Component Variation within the prior Relational structure Initial state Action interface Transition mechanism Ordered compositions drawn from 13 executable effect classes 212 tables, typed columns, and sampled foreign-key topology Fresh relational states drawn when an episode is reset 424 actions with entity, scalar, and categorical arguments Actions are governed by compositions of executable effects. The transition library spans local numeric updates and state transitions, propagation through foreign-key links, multi-row cascades, aggregate recomputation, threshold-triggered changes, stochastic and regime-dependent behavior, event creation, deletion, and delayed consequences. Relational effects can follow foreign-key paths for up to three hops and may fan out across several linked records. Delayed effects can arrive one to four steps after the action that scheduled them. Several effects may occur within the same action. They are applied in sequence to the evolving state, allowing one change to alter the conditions or inputs of another. Their target columns, coefficients, thresholds, transition maps, delays, and stochastic parameters remain fixed within world and are resampled across worlds. Direct numeric updates include additive, multiplicative, reset, and action-conditioned cross-table transformations, while aggregate effects derive values from linked records through sum, mean, max, or count. consequence can therefore combine value changes with relational propagation, state transitions, event creation, and structural effects. realized sample of 1,500 worlds from the training seed range contains 14.0 actions and 2.17 effects per action on average, producing 1.38 edits per transition. Importantly, 38.1% of realized edits occur on table other than the one directly bound by the action. separate 500-world sample from the evaluation range gives nearly identical statistics. The executable prior therefore produces substantial relational propagation in practice rather than only through rare constructed cases. E.2 Variation Across Worlds and Tasks Sampling new world changes several parts of the system at once. Its relational schema and initial-state distribution are resampled together with the action interface, the assignment from actions to mechanisms, and the parameters and composition of those mechanisms. The mechanism families and structured edit vocabulary provide common behavioral prior across worlds. Table 8 Variation between pretraining worlds and held-out WorldRel worlds. World component Held-out world Schema and foreign-key graph Initial-state distribution Table, column, category, and action identities Action argument signatures Action-to-mechanism assignment Mechanism parameters Mechanism composition Mechanism families Edit vocabulary Resampled Resampled Resampled Resampled Resampled Resampled Resampled Shared Shared Observed executions distinguish among the behaviors made possible by this prior. An action can therefore invoke different effects in different worlds, while related mechanisms can appear under different schemas, parameters, and relational bindings. The shifts in 6 probe these sources of variation separately by changing the action mapping, schema, or mechanism composition. Throughout the main evaluation, an unseen world is fresh instantiation of this executable-world prior. task draws its observed executions and query from independently reset episodes of the same world. Each world provides 20 episodes of four steps, giving up to 80 transitions from the same underlying dynamics. During pretraining, the amount of behavioral context is sampled from {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}. Drawing context across episodes exposes repeated behavior from the same world without giving the query its own execution history. 20 World generation is also separated from rendering. Schema, categorical, and action identifiers can be replaced consistently with opaque labels while preserving the relational structure, values, row identities, action bindings, and consequences. The naming experiments in 5 use this separation to vary semantic cues without changing the underlying behavioral task. E.3 Behavior Transfer Across Executions The same world-level behavior can produce different concrete edits when an action is applied in different relational state. Figure 6 shows one observed execution and query from the same world. They share an action type and transition mechanism, but bind to different records and begin from different values. Observed execution renew_shipment target=18 shipments[18] payments_id=10 is_paid=1 weight=413.523 FK payments[10] credit=8 total=325 status=refunded same action type same hidden dynamics Query in the same world renew_shipment target=4 shipments[4] payments_id=2 is_paid=0 weight=161.747 FK payments[2] credit=8 total=22 status=refunded Observed edits shipment.weight 413.523 452.001 payment.credit 8 3 Reference edits shipment.is_paid 0 1 shipment.weight 161.747 452.001 payment.credit 8 3 Figure 6 Transferring behavior across executions. The demonstrated action and the query bind to different shipment and payment rows, so the relational targets must be transferred by role rather than by row identity. The query additionally changes is_paid because its starting value differs from the demonstration. Replaying the demonstrated edit list would therefore be insufficient. The observed action changes both the targeted shipment and its linked payment. In the query, the same relational roles are occupied by different rows, so replaying the demonstrated row identities would fail. The starting state also differs, producing an additional edit to is_paid. What transfers across executions is therefore not literal edit list, but the relationship between an action, the current relational state, and the records and values it changes.
